analysis.one_liner: Bans selling essential goods at grossly inflated prices during declared shortages, with fines up to triple the revenue gained.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors on July 23, 2025 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends the Defense Production Act to make it a federal crime to sell food, medical supplies, fuel, electricity, or other essential goods at prices that 'grossly exceed' their pre-shortage levels. A price increase of 10 percent or more after the President designates a scarce material, or once an acute shortage begins, would presumptively count as price gouging. Sellers could face fines of the greater of $20,000 or three times the revenue generated from the unlawful sales, though price increases tied to legitimate business needs or costs outside the seller's control would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Households buying essential goods during emergencies — a hurricane, a pandemic, a fuel or supply-chain disruption — who today have no federal price-gouging protection and depend on a patchwork of state laws that vary in strength and coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Defense Production Act's existing ban on hoarding to also prohibit price gouging of scarce materials and any 'critical good' during an acute shortage, covering consumer food items, essential medical and emergency supplies and services, fuel, electricity, and home heating oil.

Defines an 'unfairly excessive price' as one with a gross disparity from the price immediately before a shortage begins, with a 10 percent increase treated as presumptive evidence — and explicitly allows smaller increases to still qualify.

Defines 'acute shortage' broadly to include disruptions from disease, natural disasters, military conflict, supply-chain breakdowns, and even 'extreme industry consolidation,' so protection does not depend only on a formal presidential declaration.
Imposes a criminal fine of the greater of $20,000 or 300 percent of the revenue generated in violation, making gouging financially riskier than the profit it can generate.

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of essentials — grocery stores, gas stations, pharmacies, fuel distributors — who raise prices more than marginally during shortages, and who would face fines of up to three times the revenue from those sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sellers who raise prices during shortages

drawbacks.text: The 10 percent presumptive threshold is low: even with the bill's exception for legitimate business needs and cost increases outside the seller's control, ordinary sellers could face legal risk for price changes that simply reflect higher replacement costs during a disruption.

The penalty — up to 300 percent of revenue from the unlawful sales — is steep, and the broad 'any other similar exigent constraint' language defining acute shortages gives wide discretion over when the ban switches on.

Because the prohibition is enforced through the Defense Production Act machinery, its practical reach depends on presidential designation of scarce materials and federal enforcement priorities, so coverage could be uneven even where the law is on the books.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the protection could be worth a lot during disasters, when gouging on fuel, food, and medicine is common and state laws are inconsistent. The costs fall on sellers who would have to keep prices near pre-shortage levels, and the bill does try to shield honest sellers through its business-need and cost exceptions. The main design risk is the low 10 percent trigger combined with a very large penalty, which could push sellers toward cautious, litigated pricing rather than simply deturing clear gouging.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no cosponsors and no scheduled action.

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Riley (D-NY) introduced H.R. 4720, the Cracking Down on Price Gouging Act, on July 23, 2025.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day; no markup, hearing, or vote has been scheduled since.
No other member has cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has been forced to act: sellers retain the ability to raise prices freely during shortages because no committee has moved the bill, and members of Congress face no political cost from leaving it untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sellers free to raise prices in shortages

for.name: Rep. Josh Riley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only supporter in the record so far.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or floor action have occurred and no members have cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support or opposition is not yet visible.

industries.industry: Retailers of essential goods (grocery, gas stations, pharmacies)
industries.note: The bill criminalizes raising prices more than 10 percent on food, fuel, medical supplies, and electricity during shortages, with fines up to triple the revenue gained. Only sellers who would raise prices sharply during a disruption stand to lose, and their loss is consumers' gain during emergencies; honest sellers are shielded by the bill's cost-based exceptions.

industries.industry: Fuel and home heating oil distributors
industries.note: Energy resources — fuel, electricity, heating oil — are explicitly covered critical goods, and this is the sector where shortage-driven price spikes are most common and most damaging to household budgets.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action, the realistic path for a solo-sponsor bill in Financial Services is to die there when this Congress ends. Advancing would require attracting cosponsors and persuading the committee chair to schedule a markup, neither of which has shown any sign of happening.
